subject: Heavy tailed distributions (eg Cauchy) and fast sampling

messages.author: ee490f1373633c05
messages.subject: Heavy tailed distributions (eg Cauchy) and fast sampling
parts:
Hi all,

Quick question regarding STAN and sampling from heavy tailed distributions.

I know that this is difficult for the sampler because of the non-Euclidean geometry, and that there are suggested workarounds (eg inverse transform sampling for Cauchy, mixture of normals for t distribution - although I'm not clear on whether on is generally better or not).

Suppose I have a linear regression model with coefficients {beta} and regressors {x}, and I put a Cauchy prior on the regression coefficients ie beta[i] ~ Cauchy(0, tau) for some tau. 

As the number of data points increases, should not the regression coefficients become ~ normally distributed (by the central limit theorem) and therefore the STAN sampler should not have any problems exploring the posterior?  In this scenario, do you need to worry about reparameterising the beta[i] priors (or could this even make things worse)?

Thanks

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Heavy tailed distributions (eg Cauchy) and fast sampling
parts: > I know that this is difficult for the sampler because of the non-Euclidean geometry, and that there are suggested workarounds (eg inverse transform sampling for Cauchy, mixture of normals for t distribution - although I'm not clear on whether on is generally better or not).

Clarification — the heaviness of Cauchy tails has nothing to do with wether or
not the sample space has a Euclidean geometry. The real problem is that
the heavy-tailed distributions yield heavy-tailed probability densities when
the sample space is Euclidean, and it’s the heavy-tailed density that causes
problems.

An important consequence of this more careful perspective — changing
parameters does not change the target distribution but can change the
density. Which is why the strategies you mention can improve sampling
without changing the problem.

> Suppose I have a linear regression model with coefficients {beta} and regressors {x}, and I put a Cauchy prior on the regression coefficients ie beta[i] ~ Cauchy(0, tau) for some tau.
>
> As the number of data points increases, should not the regression coefficients become ~ normally distributed (by the central limit theorem) and therefore the STAN sampler should not have any problems exploring the posterior? In this scenario, do you need to worry about reparameterising the beta[i] priors (or could this even make things worse)?

It depends on how much data you have. The more data the better
behaved the target distribution will be, but there’s no way to judge
that a priori as it will be very sensitive to your exact data.

That said, we typically recommend Gaussian priors for regression
coefficients and save Cauchy priors for regression standard
deviation.
